title: COMPOUND STIFFNESS AMPLIFICATION BY A REINFORCING RESIN
abstract: ABSTRACT                   A mechanism for amplifying the stiffness of filled rubber compounds—quantified by the dynamic storage modulus (G′)—using a resorcinol/methylene donor-type reinforcing resin (RR) has been proposed and substantiated via a series of rheological and electrical resistivity experiments. The individual and combined effects of filler and RR on G′ were systematically examined, with particular attention given to filler loading, strain-dependent G′ behavior, and the influence of filler surface characteristics. Significant amplification of low-strain G′ (LSG) by RR was observed exclusively in compounds containing interacting fillers at concentrations exceeding their percolation thresholds (typically greater than ∼12 vol%). This G′ amplification effect is further supported by rheological data obtained during vulcanization (via a moving die rheometer [MDR]) and by LSG measured on cured compounds. The extent of this influence is modulated by variations in strain amplitude during MDR testing and by the specific curing protocols used. The findings suggest that the observed increase in LSG due to RR is primarily attributable to enhanced filler network formation (EFNW). However, the EFNW capability of RR is significantly diminished when the filler surface is heavily occupied by other materials—such as hydrophobating agents used with silica—resulting in a minimal increase in LSG from RR addition. The EFNW mechanism is therefore proposed to arise from RR bridging between filler aggregates. This hypothesis is further supported by the observed decrease in electrical conductivity with increasing RR content, indicating that the conductive pathways within the filler network are disrupted by the insulating nature of RR.
